points: Failover keeps a system serving when a component dies: detect the failure, promote or route to a stand-in, and send clients to it.
The hard parts are not being fooled by a slow network, choosing exactly one replacement so there is no split-brain, and redirecting without waiting on caches.
GitHub splits database failover into detecting without false positives, deciding once with consensus, and redirecting through a proxy instead of DNS.
Amazon's static stability argues the best recovery step is one that does not have to happen, so spare capacity is held in other zones.

figures.label: 10 to 13 seconds total outage in most failover cases
50 percent extra capacity overprovisioned when using three Availability Zones

prerequisiteReasons.replication: Failover takes from replication the standby copies that are already current enough to be promoted when the primary dies.
prerequisiteReasons.consensus: Failover takes from consensus the way to choose exactly one replacement, since only one backed by a majority may take over.
prerequisiteReasons.circuit-breakers: Failover takes from circuit breakers the habit of treating a failing dependency as down and routing around it instead of waiting on it.

points: An index is a second, smaller structure kept beside the data so a query can jump to what it needs instead of reading everything.
Databases keep sorted B-tree indexes for exact lookups and ranges, and search engines keep inverted indexes mapping each word or fragment to documents.
GitHub found an index is only as good as its selectivity, and that sharding by content spreads data evenly but makes every query fan out.
Discord chooses the shard key from the query it needs: by guild for guild search, by user for searching all your DMs.

figures.label: 115 TB of original content became a 25 TB index
median query latency fell from 500 ms to under 100 ms

prerequisiteReasons.databases: Indexing takes from databases the table of rows and the queries over it, since an index is a second copy kept in step with that data.
prerequisiteReasons.sharding: Indexing takes from sharding the shard key, which decides whether a query visits one machine or all of them.

points: Load balancing spreads requests across a pool of backends so that no single instance saturates.
The hard parts are choosing which backends each client may talk to, deciding where each request goes, and reacting to load signals that are always slightly stale.
Uber found that a subsetting design needing no coordination between clients scales and fails more gracefully, and that subsets too large are safer than too small.
Dropbox advises picking a load signal that cannot look healthy while the server is stuck.

figures.label: 100,000,000 connections needed if two 10,000-task services were fully meshed
max-to-average CPU on an Envoy proxy cluster fell from 1.26 to 1.01

prerequisiteReasons.dns: Load balancing takes from DNS the idea of one name that stands for many servers, and the staleness of answers that clients keep using.

points: A message queue lets one part of a system hand work to another without waiting: producers add messages, the queue stores them, consumers take them when free.
A message can be delivered twice, late or lost, so the design says which it allows, and consumers must be safe to run twice.
Slack found that a queue keeping its backlog in memory fails exactly when it is needed most, so it put a durable log in front.
Meta's queue uses a lease plus an ack, so anything unacknowledged comes back, which makes at-least-once delivery the safe default.

figures.label: peak job rate of 33,000 per second
close to one trillion items processed per day

prerequisiteReasons.sharding: Message queues take from sharding the way one stream of work is split into partitions that separate consumers can take in parallel.
